utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can raise the blinds now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, now to your left and perhaps on the screen in front of you, you can see the Bosnian language version of your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And reflecting the question that was put to you by the Presiding Judge a few moments ago, can you now see the actual date that you provided this written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, if you could look on the hard copy that's to your left, or if the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will not be contesting the date of when the statement was given, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BQ, yesterday morning, when you arrived at the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Tribunal yesterday morning, Witness, you were given a copy of that statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to read that statement in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I read it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BQ, after reading that statement in the Bosnian language, did you have any corrections that you would like to make to that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't notice any errors that I would wish to correct. Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Witness BQ, let me ask you this question: When we reviewed your statement, when you and I reviewed your statement with a language assistant, there was one issue concerning the number of gun-shots that were fired on a particular day and you corrected part of your statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that because it said "one or more shots," but I assert it was one shot and that three people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, that is reflected on the bottom of page 7 in the English statement in the next-to-the-last paragraph. That's the point the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Witness, correct me here, but it says in the statement: "I don't know if it was one bullet that killed all three or maybe there was more than one bullet." And you corrected that to say there's no doubt in your mind that it's one bullet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was only one bullet and three people were hit. That's 100 per cent true and I guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Other than that change, Witness BQ, is there anything else that needed to be changed or corrected with respect to your February 2002 written witness statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any need to change anything or add anything, because I stand by what is in this statement and I wish my statement to remain as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it from that, sir, that there's nothing you want to add to the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to remove from the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see anything I would need to remove. It contains everything I said. I see no need either to remove anything or add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, Witness BQ, that if I were to ask you questions about the subject matters that are reflected in this written witness statement, your answers would reflect the information that's contained in that written witness statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would all be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness BQ. I have a few questions with respect to some of the locations that are mentioned in your written witness statement. Now, sir, in the English version of your statement, on page 5, you describe being taken to the police station in Prozor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown P9686, which is e-court and is also in the bundle of materials that is on the ELMO next to the witness, whichever would be quicker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are pictures from Prozor. I can see the police station, one of the restaurants, and some of the houses, and the police station is where the flag is. Here it is. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe -- I know you've mentioned the flag. Can you describe the police station building in Prozor as you see it in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the photograph you can see enough to recognise it, but -- well, it's quite easy to recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how do you recognise it in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise it by the windows. It's just the way it looks from this angle. I can recognise the side and the front. I recognise it well. I spent quite a long time there. I know every foot of the territory and the buildings and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown P9685.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the secondary school in Prozor where we were as prisoners. Yes, that's the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, that's described in your written witness statement as being the location in Prozor where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown P 08994. If that perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, this is a drawing of the secondary school. This is the layout, the disposition of the rooms. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask perhaps if the e-court version can be rotated clockwise, if that's possible, 90 degrees clockwise, that would perhaps be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BQ, just so we're absolutely clear, did you draw this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't I who drew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you recognise what this sketch depicts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because of the corridors and the way the rooms are, how they're located. If it's not identical, then at least it's very, very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BQ, in this sketch that you see before, you'll notice that the rooms are numbered. Do you know or can you recognise which room you were detained in in the Prozor secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, in room -- or rather, classroom number 9. Yes, 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown P 09718.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, sir, can you tell us, after you were detained in the secondary school, where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent a brief time in the secondary school. From there, they put us in buses and took us to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, if that photo now can be rotated counter-clockwise 90 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, do you recognise P 09718, the photograph that's before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Dretelj, and the hangars where I and the other prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say, sir, "the hangars where I and the other prisoners were," can you tell us from this photograph what you're referring to as the hangars? Perhaps describe the hangars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what words to use to describe the hangars. They look like some kind of military garage or military depot. It's not a standard building and it's not a building people can live in. To the best of my understanding, these were formerly depots or garages belonging to the former JNA or probably a weapons depot. That's what it must have been, because, as far as I was able to see, there were no conditions for people to live there or spend any amount of time in, and yet people spent several months there. The conditions were very, very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's move now, please, to P 09720.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, this is the hangar where I was put when I first arrived in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, approximately how long were you in this hangar in Dretelj that's depicted in P 09720?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the precise number of days, but it was approximately a month or maybe a few days more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BQ, after you were in this hangar for approximately a month, where did you go or where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From there I was taken through a large tunnel 200 or 300 metres away from this hangar, a huge tunnel where we were shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please now see P 09719.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember this. This is the entrance to the tunnel. You can just see the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many -- how many tunnels were there at Dretelj when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, there were two. Whether there were more than two, I wouldn't know, but I know about two tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, the tunnel you were in, is it depicted in this photo, P 09719?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there should be a road here between those two hangars, and there was one on the left and one on the right. You can see only one tunnel here, and I don't see the road leading to the hangar. But still I'm sure this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you told us a hangar on the left and a hangar on the right. Which of those two hangars were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The left one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one on the left, I think. Yes, the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please now see P 09721?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the same tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that photograph depicts, P 09721?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the tunnel where we spent a certain amount of time, I and the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you in this tunnel, Witness BQ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first hangar and in the second hangar, I spent 58 days there. I was down there for a month or so, and then up there I was some 18 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, approximately how many people were with you in this tunnel on the left-hand side in Dretelj during the time-period you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't count them, I didn't have an opportunity of counting, but I think there were between 5 and 600 at least, and there may have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other people who were with you in this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could remember a lot of names, although quite a lot of time has elapsed. And my memory has been quite poor since I was in this camp. I've had medical treatment. I might be able to remember a few names now, but I couldn't remember very many. I don't know whether you need me to mention names. I could mention a few, but not many, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, if you could mention the few names that you remember who were with you in this tunnel on the left at Dretelj, that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could remember many names. I would need time to think. It was mostly us from Prozor. In the first hangar, for a long time, there were just us from Prozor and then later on it became mixed up. There were people there from Herzegovina and even from Central Bosnia in the other place. I can only tell you the names of people from Prozor, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask the witness be shown P 03104 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness move a little closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, the interpreters are asking if you could move a little bit closer to the microphone, so if you could perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now I would ask if we could please go to the page that says "page 4" at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, on this document we see the list. Could you tell us where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document is missing apparently the first page and/or any cover page that comes with it. This document has a stamp of the Croatian state archives on the top. This is how we received the document. We do not have the pages that precede this part of the list, as we see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mundis, what do you pretend that it is? Because it has no title whatsoever. It's just a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's a list of names, Your Honours. I was going to ask the witness a question or two about the list, given that the name of the witness appears on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could look at the page, again on the bottom, bearing "page 4".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see between numbers 190 and 191 a heading on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left is the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does that heading say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, this title and this list of people is when we were released - what was the date? - when they selected a group of us for release to our territory. And I think the names you have here, it's that list of people who were released from Dretelj together with me. They never made a list of our names except then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are going to ask him if he recognises his name, you will have to move into closed session; otherwise, one could identify his name. Can we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's indulgence, I do have just a couple more questions and about four very quick photos to show the witness. I think we could probably finish before the break, but I am cognizant of the time. I anticipate we need about four to five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Finish with this and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the point I interrupted you, sir, you told us you went to Donja Dreznica. Can you tell us a little bit about what happened when you were at Donja Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Donja Dreznica we were met by an army. I didn't know who it was at the time, but it was the SFOR. There was also the International Red Cross and some Bosniak troops and people, civilians. We felt freer there. We didn't feel completely free, but we felt better at least. Our morale was higher than it had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if there were any journalists present at the time when you arrived in Donja Dreznica at the end of August 1993, with the other people from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I was so exhausted and so ill that I was unable to notice that. I didn't know what was happening around me. I just lay down on the grass waiting for someone to pick me up and take me to Jablanica where my family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown some photographs that are part of P 04588. This exhibit consists of a large number of photographs. It might very well be easier to do this on the ELMO. So perhaps the photos that are in the bundle under that exhibit number, if that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a photograph in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that this was taken in Dreznica, I'm absolutely sure, when we were resting and waiting to be transported to wherever we were destined to go. These are people I know by sight, but I'm not sure I could tell you their names correctly. However, I know most of these people by sight. As quite a lot of time as elapsed, it would be hard for me to remember their first and last names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would assist us, in order to identify the source, if the Prosecutor could explain the provenance of these photographs, because they appear to be frames from a video and we would, of course, be interested in knowing who made the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of that objection, I think we better take the recess now. These photographs were taken by a journalist. I can provide all that information after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. On the cover page, I can read "Associated Documents," so this is probably a press agency. We shall resume again at ten to 11.00 and have our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I took advantage of the break and pulled up some additional information concerning these photographs. But before I indicate the source of these documents, the Prosecution simply wants to put on the record that we don't believe, in light of the fact that the witness has identified what's contained in the photographs, that all of this is particularly necessary at this point in time. But I will proffer, for the record, that these photographs were taken by an individual named Nermin Malovic, whose name appears on the witness list in this case. We may or may not call this witness, but his name appears on the list. He was an ABiH press officer, that is, he was a photographer assigned to a unit within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The statement of Mr. Malovic, which is dated 23 and 26 November 2004, has been disclosed. He is, of course, available to the Trial Chamber as well, and that witness, in his statement, indicates and describes the situation by which he came to be at this location and took these photographs. But, again, he is on the witness list, but we might not call this person as a witness to testify. And our position clearly is that when we've had a witness describe what is contained or shown in the photographs, that that certainly is sufficient in terms of admissibility of those photographs, notwithstanding any weight that the Trial Chamber may subsequently assign to the photographs. So I put that on the record to assist the Defence and the Trial Chamber, but, again, our position at this point is that it might not absolutely be necessary with respect to the photographs. Now, again, with the assistance of the usher, if we could just return to the photographs that have been -- or the four photographs that I believe are contained in P 04588 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have not shown all the photographs. We have four. We've seen the first one, but you haven't shown all the photographs. Don't you wish to show them to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there's a translation error. I'm asking that that be done now. If we can return to the photographs P 04588.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, you commented on this photograph. Is there anything else, Witness BQ, that you would like to say about this particular photograph, the first photograph that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what I could add here. I can only see these people. They are familiar. I know them, but I can't think of anything to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next photograph in that bundle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? In the background of this photograph, behind the head of the person crouching, there is a man who has a nose which is bandaged. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what was the story of this man, why the nose was bandaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be several things, from the beating on the hills or maybe falls when we were travelling to Dreznica. I, myself, fell several times because it takes a long walk, several kilometres, and I was so exhausted I barely made it to Dreznica. I had fallen several times, so this man could have fallen, too. It could be either from beating or from falling, but it's nothing good, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused now because I thought you had told us that you were transported in trucks with a tarpaulin around it, and now you are telling us that you had to walk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We walked at Vrda, and then we had to get off the buses and walk to Dreznica. But they drove us from Capljina to Vrda, where the boundary was, the separation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would persons who got wounded during the beating be medically attended with bandages, like the one one sees on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This man could have gotten this bandage in Dreznica, not earlier, because we had nobody on the journey who could attend to anybody or help anybody, at least not that I had seen. He could have only gotten this bandage from the Red Cross in Dreznica. I don't see where else he could have gotten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one quick question from me. On the same photo we see before the first gentleman somebody who is on all fours, in white trousers on all fours. Is it because he's exhausted or because he's handicapped? Do you remember anybody who was with you there in that camp who was so exhausted that he had to walk on all fours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were some of us like that. Not only this man but there were hundreds. I told you, I could barely stand; I could barely get from Vrda to Dreznica. Some were in the same state of exhaustion; some slightly better off. But it was not infrequent that a person could not walk from exhaustion. I didn't see anybody who was really disabled. This is probably from exhaustion. I don't know what else to say on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I think the record does not reflect exactly what the witness said. Lines 17 and 19 on the previous page, he said there was nobody on the journey who could help them in terms of medical assistance. Not there; he said on the journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same goes for the place where we were in Dretelj. I had never an opportunity to see a doctor or anybody who could help those people who were in Dretelj with me. I never saw a single doctor in that compound. Whether there was anybody at all, I really couldn't say either way. But I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, perhaps if the usher could now turn to the following page and rotate that photograph, please. Sir, can you tell us anything about the photograph that you see before you now? I think actually you're covering the mirror with the top page. Witness BQ, can you tell us anything about this photograph, what it shows, who's depicted, where it's taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph was taken in Dreznica. I recognise the terrain; I recognise this location. And from what I see, these are IFOR vehicles, and you can see one of the soldiers who were there. We got refreshments there; we got water, drinks, some food. This was the first time we were able to get some sustenance. You can see a person handing out food and drinks to people who were around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, do you recognise any of the persons in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the one close up, I know him personally, by sight. But it's such a long time that I don't want to make a mistake with a name. That's why I'm going to avoid names. But I know the man from my experience, and just by this picture, I could now go to his personal address. But I wouldn't like to go into names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same photo we see one woman getting off the truck, and the soldier is helping her out. She is in a white dress. Do you know if there were any women shipped by the same trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were women from settlements in Herzegovina, in Capljina. She was not alone. There were many women and children on this truck which transported us from Capljina to Vrda, and then went on to Jablanica. There were lots of women and children and elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if we could be shown the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, I would ask you the same questions, if you can tell us anything about this photograph, such as where it was taken, when it was taken, whether you recognise anyone in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the place, but on this particular picture, from what I can see, they are mostly civilians. They're not inmates. I think those are people who travelled from Capljina with us, so it could be them on the photograph. Those are women from Capljina. I can see the old women who carried things. You see this bag next to this women. Yes, these must be the women who travelled with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BQ, you say, "I know the place." Can you tell us, what is this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the plateau of the hydro-power station in Platovice. We gathered there. We were transported by IFOR vehicles from Donja Dreznica to this plateau, and there we got schedules who would be taken where. Some were to Jablanica; some to Mostar; some to other places. But that's where we got our schedules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could be shown the last photo in this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, I'd ask you if you recognise what's depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a neighbour of mine from Varvara. You can see that he had been in a camp just like me, since his ribs are protruding this way. I can't recognise anybody else on this photograph. I know only him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, do you recognise where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say where it was taken because I can't see the location very well. I can't see the background very well because I don't see well. I just remember this man and I recognise him, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, you said on lines 17 and 18, "You can see that he'd been in a camp just like me." Do you know what camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with me certainly in the first camp, in the first hangar. I don't know where he went from there. All of us from Prozor who were bussed to Dretelj were, at first, all together in that hangar for some 20 days, after which they started placing their people from Stolac, from Mostar. But in the initial period, only we from Prozor were in this hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness BQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions. We would tender our documents at this point in time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question for you before I give the floor to the Defence counsel. In your written statement, you say that when you arrived at Dretelj you had 94 kilos, and later when you left in August you weighed only 32 kilos. I calculated you lost 60 kilos in that time; is that correct? Which means one kilo a day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as for this 32 kilos, I actually weighed 37 kilos. I don't know where this figure of 32 comes from. But it's true that I weighed 37 kilos. I weighed myself when I got to this relative in Jablanica, and I weighed 37 kilos. And I assert -- I assert with full responsibility that I weighed exactly 37 kilos when I was released from Jablanica. I may have even put on some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you eat at all during those two months; if so, what kind of food did you get and how often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we got any food, it was so awful that maybe it better we had none. My teeth used to be so good that I never had to see a dentist, and now you can see that, because of that food, I lost all my teeth; they simply crumbled. The sort of food we got, I would never have given to my dogs, my pigs, or my cattle. I would give no one and nothing that food that we got in Dretelj. And as for amounts, it was so small. One little loaf of 700 grams was divided into pieces for 17 people. And this soup that we got was just boiled over a fire and then they poured it into those dishes. I don't know what to call those dishes. And it was so hot, you know what -- how hot it can be when it's just off the fire. And we had 10, 20 seconds to eat it. I don't think anybody could have held that dish with food for more than 20 seconds. And, of course, I myself tried to eat as much of that soup as I can. That's why I lost all my teeth; now I don't have a single tooth. That's why I lost that weight. I lost my health, my memory. I lost my entire life in Dretelj. It's just that my soul hasn't yet been separated from my body. I've got nothing else left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, on the same subject, can you tell us on what the assertion when you arrived at Dretelj you weighed 94 kilos is based? Did you also weigh yourself immediately before going there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know yourself that a person always weighs themselves once a month at least. It could have been maybe not exactly 94; it could have been 96 or 92. But before that I was in Austria for 15 days. I don't know, a difference of 2 kilos more or less. But when I was released I know exactly the number on the scales was 37 kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, in light of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, good morning. You began by telling us that yesterday, when you met with the Prosecutor, you had an opportunity to read your statement twice; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time, after reading it, you saw that there was one error and you pointed that error out to the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, the Prosecutor today told us that that was, indeed, the case and then gave you an opportunity today to make any additions or retractions concerning your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, you indicated you saw no reason to make any corrections, including the one that we just saw right now when you said that you actually weighed 37. You were willing to stand by that particular assertion that you weighed actually 32.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't get to deal with every particular point yesterday, but I had to correct it now because I want to say things exactly as they were. There's not much importance to these 5 kilos. But I really want to say what happened exactly to me and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would agree with you to some extent on that. Incidentally, how much do you weigh today, right now, since I take it you measure yourself once a month, as you indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 67 kilos now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, when you were a younger man, you were much more robust, much heavier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I weighed 86 kilos when I was 18. At that time I weighed 86 kilos and I was not as weak as I am now. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- really hard-working when I was a young man. I wouldn't have much to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The point I want to get to in your -- is with respect to your testimony today, when you were released from Dretelj. Today you told us that before being released you were -- you and others were beaten. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember because that was that last moment of our stay in Dretelj, just before they loaded us on to vehicles. Not only just me but all the others. Seven or eight soldiers walked among us and beat whoever they could lay their hands on, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. You were rather descriptive in your testimony and that's what caught my attention. Because when I look at your statement, you do mention of other incidents of mistreatment, yet on page 8 in the English version - I don't know what the page is on the B/C/S version - there's absolutely no mention of any beatings prior to being released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you did not find it, I don't think you read my statement, because it's right here in the statement, in the report which is in front of me, and it's accurate. I think you will read there that they kicked us, they beat us with their rifles and the sticks, the handles of shovels, and many other instruments that we were beaten with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I missed it. But the portion I'm looking at is on page 8, and I'll just read it in English. It says: "I was released from Dretelj on 28th August 1993. On that day, about 5 to 6.000 prisoners were released. They were all elderly, very young or those in the poorest conditions. They put us on trucks and buses to Vrda near Dreznica where the front line was. We walked across the bridge in Dreznica to where our army was waiting." That's the passage that I see with respect to August 28th, the date of your release. Now, as I indicated, sir, while you mentioned previous abuses while you were staying there, there's absolutely nothing in your statement with respect to any abuse upon your release.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you missed one word in that statement. Not 5, 6.000, but 500, 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're right. You're absolutely correct. Thank you. My eyesight is going bad. Thank you for correcting me. Since you found -- you were able to correct me on that, I take it you were also able to see that there is nothing about beatings or mistreatment prior to being released in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you either misread it, but it's mentioned in that statement that I gave in Mostar. The beatings are mentioned. I don't know how well you read it, how thoroughly you read it, but there are references to abuse and to beatings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: One moment, and I apologise for interrupting you, Mr. Karnavas. If I'm not mistaken, you said that there is nothing about beatings or mistreatment prior to being released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the day of release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: On the day, yes. But let me draw your attention, sir, to page 8 of the statement, then around the middle of that, we will see really - one, two, three, four - in the fifth paragraph, five, and it is being read, and I quote: "Personally I was beaten many times. Sometimes I would not be beaten up for a week, and then on other occasions I would get beaten several times a day. There was talk that some people were forced to do sexual acts, but I didn't see it," et cetera. So then here in the first two sentences there are references to beatings, so it is what -- I saw some problems when you mentioned that in your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, again -- yeah, Your Honour, it was just a point of precision. I'm not contesting the fact that he wasn't beaten. It's just that that one instance sticks out. Because he's so careful in all other acts of mistreatment - and we're not contesting that - but on this particular occasion of being released, he mentions -- and there's nothing in the statement. It would be page 13 on the B/C/S version. I just point that out for the Court's attention, for whatever it is worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one last question, sir, did you mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll clarify that. Witness, you have heard counsel, who rightly says that in your statement this incident wherein you were beaten before getting on the truck is not specifically recounted. My colleague on the Bench tells me that two paragraphs earlier you explained that you were beaten repeatedly. Now, to the best of your recollection - although I understand that it's been a long time, but such things remain etched in one's memory - when you spoke -- when you were interviewed by the investigator of the Tribunal, did you really tell him everything, all about this in detail? And is it him who synthesised all this information, who summarised this in one sentence, "I was beaten many times"? Is that the way it happened with your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, these questions have come up now about the transport from Dretelj to Dreznica, and it's possible that, when I was giving that statement in Mostar, it was not recorded or maybe I didn't tell the investigator specifically what happened on the transport from Dretelj to Dreznica. Maybe different questions were asked then than the questions that were asked now. But I am answering now the questions that are being asked now, and I'm telling the truth. And if there is something suspicious or dubious about my account of the trip from Vrda to Dreznica, you can find a hundred witnesses to corroborate what I'm saying. I am now answering questions directly. Maybe the investigator who took this statement didn't ask me specifically what happened from Capljina to Vrda or from Vrda to Dreznica until you got to your own army. So the things that are being asked today are not necessarily the same that were being asked then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just a short question for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Just one small point. On page 8 of your statement given to investigators in Mostar for this Tribunal - in English it's on page 5, the third whole paragraph on the page; in the Croat version, it's paragraph 2 on page 8 - I will read to you exactly the sentence that you wrote. It's after those events in the village in October 1992. At the end of that passage you say the following: "Things went back to normal and I thought everything was going to be all right. I was not scared that something would happen, because on the news they said that the fighting in Prozor had been a mistake that would not be repeated." Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Just a few hours before that statement I had arrived from Austria, and since I was not in town, I was not able to know who exactly is saying what. I just heard from people, from both Muslims and Croats, or Catholics, whatever, that some session was being held in Prozor, that they are not able to agree, the people holding that session. All these were stories circulating in the village and people were seized by panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've already explained that. Just give me a precise answer. You don't have to give me the whole story. On the news -- just now you said it was something you heard from other people, but here in the statement you say "on the news." Do you mean on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't have occasion to listen to the radio. I mean the news that you get from people, from one person to another. I heard that it was a mistake. After the conflict, however, I heard on the news that it was a mistake. But before the conflict, I was not able to hear anything because I don't think the media was reporting anything. Just after the conflict, they said it was a mistake, it was not a major incident, just a conflict among the citizens. And I was seriously injured; I was lying in the house of one neighbour, a Catholic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said all that in your statement. We don't need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm to you now that that's the way it happened. Just ask me directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have now discovered where the misunderstanding lies. So after those events in the course of 1992, what you've just mentioned, "they said on the news that fighting in Prozor have been a mistake that would not be repeated," tell me just about that, very simply. When you say "on the news" here, do you mean news on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, so it's television. That's what they said on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a statement from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you heard that on news, on TV news, that the fighting in Prozor had been a mistake that would not be repeated. That's what they reported on TV. Is that correct; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on TV, because they made an appeal to the citizens of Prozor to come back to their homes because it would not be repeated. And then people who were able to return returned. And I was unable because I was lying in the house of that Croat neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. After that, as you said in the next passage in your statement, everything was all right until the 4th of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a few short questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day to you. I am Vesna Alaburic, an attorney from Zagreb. And in these proceedings I appear for General Milivoj Petkovic. I will put a few questions to you with reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. The last response given by the witness has not entered the record. In his last reply, after my question, he confirmed that everything was all right until the 4th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: They did not hear the witness's reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my last question to you was: As of the 4th of July, 1993, everything was peaceful, as you said in your statement; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, a few questions about the events in your village in October 1992. On page 7 of your statement, which is page 5 in the English text, you said, and I quote: "The fighting did not last long because the Muslims were unable to defend themselves." Could you please now explain what kind of weapons the Muslims had at that point in time and why was it they were not able to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for certain that in October 1992 a large number of people from my hamlet, and even from Prozor, were unarmed and not prepared. We were not expecting any kind of conflict between the Bosniaks and the Croats. And I am sure they did not have weapons. They might have had a rifle or an automatic rifle, but there were so few weapons they're not even worth mentioning. If we had been attacked by only 20 soldiers, the Muslims would not have been prepared to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did any of the people in your village have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask: Could witness's other microphone be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know only one man in my village who had a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there were two hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat your answer to this question because your microphone was not on. My question was: Did you know anyone who had weapons among the people in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in my village I know only one man who had a Kalashnikov, that's an automatic rifle, and there were two hunting rifles. Those were the weapons I knew about in my village before these conflicts and on the day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the name of the person who had a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you to stop, because if the name would have been mentioned, one could have identified him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session? I believe it might be useful for purposes of clarifying the events in the village if we were to find out who was the person who had the Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us who this person was? And it will be up to Their Honours to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, I give the floor to the Prosecution so that it can give us a list of the documents it wishes to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would tender the following documents and photographs which have been shown to the witness during the course of his testimony: P 09716, under seal; P 03104, under seal; P 04588; P 08994; P 09685; P 09686; P 09718; P 09720; P 09719; and P 09721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections from the Defence? No objection from the part of the Defence. So the exhibits under these numbers are admitted. P 03104, under seal; P 09716 under seal; P 09718, P 09720; P 09719; and P 09721. I believe one is missing. I read too quickly. P 045808 and 508994 [as interpreted]. The court reporters made a mistake it's P 08994. It's P 08994. I would like the Legal Officer to check that nothing has been missed out. Witness, your testimony has come to an end. I'd like to thank you for having come to testify, as was requested by the Prosecution, about those events that unfolded in your country. On behalf of the Bench, we wish you a safe journey home. Before you leave the courtroom, I shall ask the usher to drop the blinds, please. I would like to add that the registrar has told me, I don't understand why the court reporter has not put in all those numbers. We need to add P 09686 and P 09685.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, I think there may be one other error. I see at line 9, the number P 045808 I think that should be P 04588, if Mr. Mundis confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So it's Exhibit number P 04588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall move back into open session. You can lift the blinds now since there is no witness in the courtroom. Mr. Mundis, before we have a break and before the end of this hearing, because we are going to be holding another hearing after this one, as far as next week is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Everything is as per the court schedule with respect to next week. We have the witness who is returning for cross-examination, followed by four crime base witnesses who will be testifying for the duration of the week next week. There are no changes to the schedule as previously circulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. As far as Tuesday's witnesses are concerned, I think you'd planned to lead him for two hours. I think if it's two hours, that's going to be short, if we have the cross-examination on the same day, which means that we will probably have to hear the witness on the Wednesday as well. But maybe it will be shorter than those two hours which you have announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I believe I speak for all the Prosecution team when I say we're constantly trying to slim down the amount of time spent on direct examination, to the greatest extent possible. The witness appearing is a crime base victim witness, and I don't believe that we'd have any problems finishing her testimony in one complete day, in light of the fact that the Defence tend to take slightly less time than they're allotted with respect to crime base witnesses, as a general rule, at least based on what's happened thus far in the course of the trial. So I don't anticipate any problems. You'll also note on Thursday of next week we have one 92 ter witness scheduled, so there is a little bit of flexibility, if we run into some problems in the middle part of the week, with respect to finalising the witnesses that we do have scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one issue. While I was away, apparently - I was absent from the courtroom - there was some indication from Mr. Mundis himself as to how far along they were in their case. I believe he had indicated something to the effect, about a quarter of the way through. In light of the fact that, as I understand, the registrar has allotted 12 months and two weeks for this phase of the case, it would assist the Defence if, at some point, the Prosecution could figure out exactly how far along and when do they predict are they going to be on schedule. I know we're counting hours as opposed to months and weeks, but it would assist us for other purposes. And we're not trying to rush them through their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, right. I think that would be useful to everybody because it's a question that I have already discussed with the Judges. Maybe it's too early, but, Mr. Mundis, do you have an idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if the registrar has convenient the amount of hours that we've spent total to date, that might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I asked for it last time, registrar, I asked for a calculation of hours. Maybe it's between 80 or 100 hours used by the Prosecution from the beginning, but I need an exact total, not today but you have all of the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can assure the Defence and the Trial Chamber that being allotted 400 hours, I don't believe at this point in time that we're going to be completing our case in 200 hours or 220 hours. I anticipate that -- that we've used, by our count, about 83 hours. That is a little bit less than 25 per cent of the time we've been allotted. Barring any unforeseen circumstances, it would appear that we will be taking the full 400 hours that we have been allotted, which we have been planning on and which we have relied upon in terms of structuring our case. That's about all I can say at this point in time. If Your Honours would like a more full explanation, we might be in a position to prepare something that we could do at some point in the near future. But I need to be very clear that we will be taking the full amount of time that the Trial Chamber has allocated to us. We will be taking that figure of 400 hours for direct examination and factor that into all of our planning, and we have relied upon that figure for purposes of structuring the Prosecution case. So I don't believe that we'll be in a position to significantly reduce that number, and we're not intending on doing so. But again, if it would be helpful to the Chamber, I'll discuss with my colleagues and we can perhaps have a discussion with a little more preparation in the very near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but everybody should have a document to know where we are going and not to go straight into a wall. We need to have an overall document to see, one, if you are behind your schedule - I don't think you are - if are following a good tempo and to give time to the Defence to prepare themselves. They have a lot of work to do and they have to prepare cross-examination, and they have to also prepare their Defence case. For that it is necessary to have certain parameters that would allow everybody to work well and usefully. If there are no other matters to raise, we are going to adjourn now, and we will continue in ex parte in 30 minutes. So I invite you all to come back here again on Monday, at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.05 p.m.,
